---
title: "Introduction"
author: "Anselm Jeong"
date: "2026-01-26"
format: docx
bibliography: "Metaplasticity.bib"
---

A growing body of evidence indicates that several psychiatric treatments, including electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), psychedelics such as ketamine, and antidepressants like SSRIs, share a common mechanistic foundation: the enhancement of neuroplasticity. Despite their disparate delivery methods and temporal profiles, each of these modalities has been shown to promote synaptogenesis, upregulate neurotrophic signaling, and induce structural and functional changes in brain networks. This convergence on neuroplasticity as a final common pathway has prompted a reconceptualization of these interventions, viewing them not merely as neurotransmitter-modulating agents but as catalysts for neural circuit reorganization. Accordingly, this paper will refer to ECT, psychedelics, and traditional antidepressants collectively as "neuroplasticity-enhancing treatments" (NPETs).

In clinical practice, however, no single NPET consistently achieves satisfactory treatment outcome on its own. ECT, for example, can induce remission in a sizable proportion of treatment-resistant depression, yet up to 84% of remitted patients relapse within six months without maintenance pharmacotherapy [@sackeimEtAl2001]. Conversely, regardless of the duration of administration, SSRIs often lack the potency to elicit response in more than half of the patients [@rush2020]. These limitations have led clinicians to combine NPETs, such as ECT with antidepressants, or psychedelics with psychotherapy. Yet not all combinations of NPETs produce the desired results. Some may be redundant, while others may even prove antagonistic. Timing and sequence also matter. For example, when antidepressants were initiated concurrently with ECT rather than after its completion, remission rates were approximately 15% higher [@sackeimEtAl2009].

Yet combination strategies remain largely empirical, relying on trial-and-error rather than solid principles. If combination strategies are to move beyond this empirical stage, a deeper understanding of each treatment's unique mechanism is required: the specificity of its effects, the temporal dynamics of its action, and which phase of the treatment process it primarily serves. Each modality possesses distinct strengths and limitations. ECT and psychedelics deliver powerful but transient perturbations. SSRIs provide gentle, sustained scaffolding but lack disruptive force. Designing synergistic combinations demands a theoretical framework that can integrate these complementary profiles.

To date, no unified theoretical framework has been proposed that encompasses all NPETs. A useful starting point, however, can be found in the model of ECT proposed by Ousdal et al. [@ousdalEtAl2022]. They formulated the action of ECT as a multiphase process of disruption, potentiation, and rewiring (DPR). In this model, a powerful perturbation temporarily destabilizes global neural circuits, opening a window of heightened plasticity that provides scaffolds for the new neural configurations [@erchinger2023]. Notably, this conceptualization converges seamlessly with the dynamical systems perspective on psychopathology, which views mental disorders as the system being trapped in pathological attractor states within a multidimensional state space [@schefferEtAl2024a; @schefferEtAl2024b]. From this vantage point, treatment resistance reflects entrapment in a deep pathological attractor, and relapse represents the system's return to that attractor after a temporary escape that was not sufficiently consolidated.

Yet the DPR model, as originally formulated, does not fully account for the maintenance of therapeutic gains. Even when disruption, potentiation, and rewiring successfully reconfigure the attractor landscape, the newly established healthy state remains fragile unless the brain's intrinsic capacity for self-regulation is restored. Homeostatic plasticity—the suite of compensatory mechanisms by which neurons and circuits maintain stable activity levels—may provide such stabilizing function [@turrigiano2011]. Within the dynamical systems framework, this restorative capacity corresponds to what Scheffer et al.[@schefferEtAl2024a] describe as "healthy resilience." It denotes the deepening and widening of the healthy basin of attraction. When homeostatic regulation is intact, the system possesses the resilience to absorb minor perturbations without slipping back into pathological attractors. When it is compromised, the healthy basin remains shallow, and even modest stressors can precipitate relapse. Based on this, we extend the DPR framework by appending a fourth phase (homeostasis) and propose the Disruption–Potentiation–Rewiring–Homeostasis (DPRH) model.

The present paper advances a dual argument. First, we examined the theoretical plausibility of the DPRH model through the lens of accumulated evidence from neuroplasticy studies, functional and structural connectivity studies, and dynamical systems theory. Second, we tried to explore the position and role of each treatment within the DPRH model. On this basis, we tried to develop a rationale for combination strategies, arguing that optimal strategies should pair interventions whose temporal profiles and mechanistic strengths complement one another across the full DPRH sequence.
